title: Everything is overdue: choose the first useful action
dek: Check serious consequences first, separate real deadlines from guilt, and turn one overdue obligation into a specific action or request for help.
metaDescription: Start an overdue backlog by checking safety and hard deadlines, verifying consequences, contacting the right person and recording one next action.

paragraphs: When everything is overdue, first check for immediate safety issues, serious consequences and hard deadlines. Then choose one item based on what happens next if it waits, verify the relevant facts and take its smallest useful action. Do not prioritize only by who is chasing you: a quiet court notice or insurance deadline may matter more than a persistent routine email.

A backlog can make every item feel equally late. The unpaid bill, appointment request and unanswered friendly message all acquire the same weight. The first job is to separate their actual consequences, not solve the whole list. This is practical triage, not legal advice, financial advice or treatment for difficulty starting tasks.

body.heading: Run a short consequence check
items: Look for danger, threatened loss of housing or essential service, court notices and urgent health administration.
Read the actual date and required action on each consequential notice.
Check uncertain deadlines through official channels rather than assuming a missed date makes action pointless.
Write what happens if each remaining item waits until the next planned session.
Choose the most consequential time-sensitive item, not automatically the oldest or quickest.
Name the first useful action: open the notice, find the account, ask a question or submit a complete response.
Record the next step, owner and date before switching tasks.

body.heading: Invented example: four late items are not equal
rows: Read the notice and contact qualified local help promptly
Contact the provider about options and requirements
Send a brief acknowledgement when urgent items are contained
Verify policy and whether an eligible return can still be made

body.heading: Late is a prompt to check, not a diagnosis of the outcome
paragraphs: Do not infer fees, credit reporting or legal consequences from the number of days alone. Different accounts and notices have different terms. A phone bill being twelve days late does not establish whether a fee was charged, service is at risk or a balance was referred elsewhere. Read the account and ask the provider.

If a date has passed, ask what options remain and whether anything must still be submitted. Do not assume there is a grace period; do not assume there is none. Record the answer and seek qualified advice when rights or serious consequences are involved. A representative's informal reassurance may not amend a written deadline.

The [CFPB behind-on-bills booklet](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_your-money-your-goals_behind-on-bills_booklet_cobrand.pdf) includes tools for prioritizing payments by consequences and contacting creditors. That is a better foundation than treating the loudest reminder as automatically the most important bill.

items.line: I am checking the status of this account. What is currently due, what consequence or date applies next, and what options are available? Please explain any fees or conditions and how I can get the arrangement in writing.
I have not completed this yet. I can send [specific part] by [realistic time]. Would that meet your need, or is there a deadline I should understand first?
Can you sit with me while I open this notice? I need to identify who sent it, what it requires and the date. I am not asking you to solve the whole backlog.

body.heading: Make the first action complete enough to matter
paragraphs: Opening a portal can be a starting movement, but it is not the same as submitting a form. If the obligation is urgent, use that movement to reach a meaningful checkpoint: identify the deadline, make the contact or gather the required response. Record what remains so a tiny first step does not become a reason to leave a serious item unattended.

For routine work, a small step may be enough for the session. A first draft of a message, a located reference number or a document placed beside the form can reduce the next barrier. The [first physical step examples](/guides/first-physical-step-20-examples) distinguish an observable starting action from a vague project name.

Keep a separate waiting list when the next action belongs to someone else. Add when you contacted them and the promised response date. Waiting is not finished, but it is also not a task to repeat every hour. Follow up based on the actual deadline and consequence.

body.heading: Stop the session deliberately, not automatically
paragraphs: Before stopping, check that no other known serious deadline will pass before you return. If several need action, ask for practical help or advice instead of assuming one task per day is always enough. A short-session method must not override safety or external deadlines.

For the rest, record one next review and the location of the list. If difficulty managing ordinary obligations persists or affects health, work or basic care, consider professional support. This workflow can organize a backlog, but cannot explain its cause or replace that support.

items.q: Should I do the easiest overdue task first?
items.a: Only after checking consequences and deadlines. An easy task can help you begin, but it should not displace an urgent notice or an essential payment problem. If a consequential item is too difficult, make its first action asking the appropriate person for help.

items.q: What if the deadline has already passed?
items.a: Check the notice and contact the relevant organization or qualified adviser promptly. There may still be a required response or available option, but do not assume an extension or grace period. Record what you learn, including any remaining date and the evidence for it.

items.q: Can I stop after one thing?
items.a: For routine backlog work, yes, once you have a clear next step. First check that no known serious deadline or safety issue will be left unattended until your return. The aim is a manageable session, not a rule that urgent obligations must wait until tomorrow.

visuals.title: Consequence before task size

steps.label: Protect
steps.detail: Check danger, housing, essential services and serious notices first.

steps.label: Verify
steps.detail: Read actual dates and requirements instead of inferring them from lateness.

steps.label: Act
steps.detail: Choose one useful action or request for appropriate help.

visuals.caption: The oldest, easiest and loudest tasks are not necessarily the most urgent.
visuals.alt: Overdue tasks are filtered by safety and consequences, verified deadlines and then a useful next action.

visuals.title: Know where the work stands

steps.label: Needs action
steps.detail: A defined step belongs to you and has a relevant date.

steps.label: Waiting
steps.detail: Someone else has the next step and a follow-up is recorded.

steps.label: Deferred
steps.detail: The task can wait until a named review without a known serious consequence.

visuals.caption: Deferred does not mean forgotten, and waiting does not mean complete.
visuals.alt: An overdue record separates tasks requiring action, replies awaited and safely deferred items with review dates.

research.intent: Triage a mixed backlog without letting small-step advice delay serious obligations.
